result.summary: This PR fixes a crash in the transaction orphanage where dividing a global latency score among more than 3000 peers with orphan announcements produces a zero per-peer allowance, triggering an assertion abort during trimming. It floors the per-peer latency share at one and makes peers at that minimum eligible for eviction, restoring the orphanage's ability to return to its global limit. The change includes a regression unit test, expanded fuzz coverage for the zero-share case, and documentation updates clarifying the actual eviction guarantees.
result.problem: Nodes configured with very high peer counts (achievable on stock Linux via raised file descriptor limits, though capped below this on select()-based builds like macOS) can trigger an integer-division-by-zero condition in orphanage trimming that aborts the node, a denial-of-service and stability risk for operators running high-connection nodes.

result.card: This PR fixes a node-crashing assertion abort in the transaction orphanage that occurs when more than 3000 peers have orphan announcements, causing integer division to produce a zero per-peer latency allowance during trimming. The fix floors the per-peer share at one and makes peers at that floor eligible for eviction, restoring correct trimming behavior; jeanpablojp independently reproduced the crash on master with a small repro (global limit 2, three peers) confirming the bug is real and the two-part fix (floor plus inclusive comparison) is necessary together. Review involved three members (jeanpablojp, brunoerg, danielabrozzoni) who requested doc clarifications, added fuzz coverage of the zero-share path, and a missing sanity check, all of which the author addressed via force-pushes on the same day, leaving the PR at Strong agreement and Ready for review. No dependencies; two unrelated open PRs touch overlapping files but are not blocking. Impact is a stability/DoS fix for nodes reachable at unusually high peer counts (above default limits, achievable on Linux with raised file descriptor limits), which caps this as P2 rather than P1 in p2p.
